For example, if I hit 200 comment CP, I would then be eligible to create a verse and be added to the mod team of an already existing verse. If after "spending" those comment CP's, I tried to create and mod another verse, I wouldn't be allowed to do so.

That it does.

I'm not discounting the idea but as someone who has moderated a number of forums in the past, there are so many easy ways to circumvent this. On forums, we'd get a lot of "me too" comments that would increase the user's post count and quickly elevate them into the next tier. I could see /v/circlejerk used for something like this too. Something to think about.

Maybe in Atko's spare time, he could whip up a top-secret super algorithm that combines account age, number of submissions (content and comments), as well as submission and comment CP into a magic number that determines someone's eligibility to moderate.

Not sure how feasible, but how about also considering how many different people actually give points to a user?

What I mean by that is, if we want to measure how much someone is contributing to whoaverse, a small group of people circle-jerking amongst themselves for points should not have the same 'score' as someone who gets points from a larger set of users as a result of submitting good content/comments.

I'd also restrict it to CP that's earned within the verse. This way, you avoid karma whores who can then become power mods. Otherwise a successful karma whore who's a master at posting witty quips at high traffic times becomes a huge mod, which is basically the same as Reddit.

On another note, may I request that we change the term CP? You know... CP... cheese pizza, uhh...

Anyway, I'm thinking that if you're modding a verse with a lot of activity, you need to maybe earn at least 10 CP a month or something (there could also be "mod action points" that are awarded to behind-the-scenes mod work like answering mod mail or something - but that would have to have measures to avoid being gamed, of course) to retain the right to mod. In a verse with less activity where in a typical month just ~50 CP are given out, then 10 CP is way too high a bar, so then make the requirement 10 comments a month or something like that (no CP requirement, just comment activity).

In order to make sure it isn't a bunch of people circle-jerking, maybe 1. CP gained from other mods upvoting you doesn't count and 2. If the same user upvotes you more than once, every subsequent upvote gets you less CP, until maybe the 6th upvote from the same user within a month provides 0 CP for the calculation of the mod's right to remain.

The numbers are all just conjecture. But the point I'm trying to make is that the mod of /v/TheFappening shouldn't be able to retain his right to mod there if he hasn't done anything there and spends all his time on /r/news. Currently, /v/TheFappening is very happening (heh) so their mods should make sure to be involved by earning CP or mod action points. In a year from now, it's doubtful /v/TheFappening will be very active, maybe < 5 CP per month are given out. Then, make the requirement basically 0 CP/mod action points for the mod to be able to remain, since a dead verse doesn't really need an active mod.

Microsoft is killing the Nokia and Windows Phone brands
I think the article's title is a bit misleading, it implies that microsoft will kill windows phone, but they're only changing the name to windows.
I used the original title, but I agree, it is a bit misleading.

It does say "brands" right there are the end. Functionally literate people can suss out the meaning.

That said, this is an interesting change of the sort we've seen a lot of since Nadella took over. Lumia is a much stronger brand for phones than Nokia and "Windows" alone goes over much better than "Windows" followed by basically any qualifier (it's like when people start rolling their eyes).

I have a theory that Windows mobile apps are going to blow up in the near future. There's a ton of discussion about the over-saturation and commensurate invisibility on the App Store and Google Play. If a developer has a really good idea the problem is getting noticed. Solution is to develop it on Windows where it can get a ton of attention if it's really good. This is kind of how Angry Birds took off - it was the earliest fully-realized game that was any fun. Once you get hyped on Windows the name will be out there and you can drop your Android and IOS versions and rake in the cash.
I think this is a smart move by Microsoft. They really need to shorten up the names and make it less confusing for customers. This is a good decision.
